stories.title: Somali Disaster Agency Delivers NFIs to Vulnerable Households in Bay Region
stories.description: BAIDOA, The Somali Disaster Management Agency (SoDMA) has distributed non-food items to displaced families and vulnerable communities in Baidoa, in the Bay region of South West State, according to officials who monitored the distribution. The supplies included rainproof sheets, mosquito nets, and other essential items intended to meet the basic needs of families living in displacement camps and vulnerable households in the city. The distribution was attended by Baidoa District Deputy Commissioner for Social Affairs Adow Aden Nur, a representative from the South West State Ministry of Humanitarian Affairs, and SoDMA’s Emergency Response and Recovery Adviser, Muqtaara Sheikh Hussein. Displacement Pressure Mounts as El Niño Flood Risk Looms The assistance comes as Baidoa continues to absorb significant numbers of newly displaced people while facing an additional threat from projected El Niño-related flooding. Baidoa is among 29 districts across 14 regions that SoDMA has identified for heightened preparedness ahead of the Deyr rainy season, as FTL Somalia reported. The agency has warned that 2.5 to 3.5 million people could be exposed to flooding nationwide, with approximately 1 million likely to be displaced. More than 14,800 people were newly displaced in Baidoa between January and September 2026, part of a broader pattern that has seen over 774,000 people displaced across Somalia during the same period. The International Organization for Migration has warned that nearly 874,000 people could be displaced nationwide between October and December, with flooding accounting for 92 percent of projected displacement, as FTL Somalia reported. IOM has trained 129 community volunteers in Baidoa specifically to help displaced and host communities prepare for El Niño-related flooding. Humanitarian agencies activated a Floods Anticipatory Action Implementation Plan ahead of the projected rains, backed by $7 million from the Central Emergency Response Fund and a further $1 million from the Somalia Humanitarian Fund. stories.title: Early face-experience deprivation leads to long-lasting deficits in macaque cortical face processing
stories.description: Experience-dependent plasticity in early sensory cortex is restricted to critical periods early in development. Whether plasticity in higher-order cortex is similarly restricted remains unclear. In the primate ventral visual stream, face-selective cortex emerges with experience during development, providing a powerful system to test how the timing of experience shapes higher-order representations. Using three male rhesus macaques selectively deprived of early face experience followed by prolonged normal face exposure, we found that face-experience-deprived monkeys acquire face-directed viewing behavior and neural face selectivity. However, they showed atypical within-face viewing patterns, while their neural representations retained lasting signatures of early deprivation, including selectivity for both faces and hands and reduced discrimination for face identity, expression, and viewpoint. Thus, higher-order visual cortex remains plastic beyond early development, yet the timing of experience fundamentally constrains the refinement of later-acquired neural representations. The emergence of category selectivity is not fully understood. Sharma and Livingstone show that when face experience is delayed in macaques, higher-order visual cortex remains plastic beyond early development, but the resulting neural representations do not develop typically.

stories.title: Probabilistic resilience mapping to flooding of urban multi-infrastructure systems
stories.description: Because they are highly interdependent, most infrastructure systems are vulnerable to disasters such as severe floods. A vast amount of data has been made available with which to better anticipate the impact of severe floods and enable areas prone to flooding to become more sustainable and resilient. However, integrating these data sources and modelling the impact of floods remains challenging. In this study, we develop a transferable, fact-calibrated, weakly supervised, physically constrained probabilistic modelling framework designed to address this issue. We estimate the facility level flood risk during a flood by integrating XGBoost and depth damage functions. Furthermore, we use Granger tests, distributed-lag models, and spatiotemporal Durbin specifications to examine cross system predictive temporal dependencies and finite-horizon lag patterns. The study offers three main findings. First, flood-induced damage exhibits a threshold-driven structure: damage across all infrastructure types is activated within a narrow depth band ( ~ 0.20–0.26 m), suggesting universal hydraulic tipping points for sustainable infrastructure management. Second, at the predictive temporal dependence level, cross system associations are more selective than the underlying physical connections suggest. Rather than being widely distributed, these associations are concentrated around a limited set of potential bridging nodes, providing a basis for targeted resilience interventions in urban contexts. Third, temporal risk dynamics exhibit systematic differences in response latency and finite-horizon risk signal persistence across infrastructure types.
